library(ggplot2)
library(dlm)
library(knitr)

y <- datasets::Nile

nile_data <- data.frame(
  Year = as.numeric(time(y)),
  Flow = as.numeric(y)
)

V_known <- 15100
W_known <- 1470
m0 <- 1000
C0 <- 1000

nile_model <- dlmModPoly(
  order = 1,
  dV = V_known,
  dW = W_known,
  m0 = m0,
  C0 = C0
)
```

# Introduction

This analysis uses a dynamic linear model to describe changes
in the underlying level of annual Nile flow. We distinguish
sequential state estimation through Kalman filtering,
one-step-ahead prediction, and retrospective reconstruction
through smoothing.

We also examine sensitivity to the signal-to-noise ratio,
check standardized forecast errors, and estimate the observation
and state innovation variances by maximum likelihood.

# Data and Model Specification

The Nile dataset, included in R, contains 100 annual observations
of river flow at Aswan from 1871 to 1970, measured in
$10^8\,\mathrm{m}^3$. The series shows a marked decline around
the end of the nineteenth century.

```{r nile-series-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=2, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Annual Nile flow at Aswan, 1871–1970. Data are available in R through the Nile dataset."}
ggplot(nile_data, aes(x = Year, y = Flow)) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#243746",
    linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#243746",
    size = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1880, 1960, 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = expression("Annual flow (" * 10^8 * " " * m^3 * ")")
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )
```

We use a local level model, also called a random walk plus noise:

\[
\begin{aligned}
y_t &= \theta_t + v_t,
& v_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,V),\\
\theta_t &= \theta_{t-1} + w_t,
& w_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,W).
\end{aligned}
\]

The observation errors and state innovations are independent
over time and mutually independent, and are independent of
the initial state.

For the initial analysis, the variances are treated as fixed
at \(V=15100\) and \(W=1470\), with initial distribution

\[
\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(1000,1000),
\]

where the second parameter is the variance.
The latent level can change over time, although the model
does not explicitly specify a discrete change point.

# Kalman Filtering

The Kalman filter updates the estimated level as each observation
becomes available. The filtering distribution is

\[
\theta_t \mid y_{1:t} \sim \mathcal{N}(m_t,C_t),
\]

where \(m_t\) is the estimated level and \(C_t\) measures its
remaining uncertainty after observing \(y_t\).

```{r kalman-filter}
nile_filter <- dlmFilter(y, nile_model)

filter_mean <- as.numeric(dropFirst(nile_filter$m))

filter_covariances <- dlmSvd2var(
  nile_filter$U.C,
  nile_filter$D.C
)

filter_variance_all <- vapply(
  filter_covariances,
  function(x) as.numeric(x[1, 1]),
  numeric(1)
)

filter_variance <- filter_variance_all[-1]
filter_sd <- sqrt(filter_variance)

filter_data <- data.frame(
  Year = nile_data$Year,
  Flow = nile_data$Flow,
  Mean = filter_mean,
  SD = filter_sd,
  Lower = filter_mean - qnorm(0.975) * filter_sd,
  Upper = filter_mean + qnorm(0.975) * filter_sd
)

stopifnot(
  length(filter_mean) == length(y),
  length(filter_variance_all) == length(y) + 1,
  all(is.finite(filter_mean)),
  all(is.finite(filter_variance)),
  all(filter_variance > 0)
)
```

```{r filtering-uncertainty-plot, fig.height=1.5, fig.cap="Filtering standard deviation of the latent level, conditional on the specified variances and initial distribution."}
ggplot(filter_data, aes(x = Year, y = SD)) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#243746",
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1880, 1960, 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Filtered state SD"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
```

The filtering standard deviation initially increases and then
stabilizes. The initial variance is below its steady-state value:
new observations reduce uncertainty, but state innovations
introduce additional uncertainty at every step. Consequently,
the filtering variance does not converge to zero.

```{r filtered-level-plot, fig.cap="Observed Nile flow and filtered latent level. The shaded band gives pointwise 95 percent credible intervals for the state, conditional on the specified model parameters."}
ggplot(filter_data, aes(x = Year)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper),
    fill = "#24476B",
    alpha = 0.16
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Flow, color = "Observed flow"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Mean, color = "Filtered level"),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed flow" = "#999999",
      "Filtered level" = "#24476B"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1880, 1960, 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = expression("Annual flow (" * 10^8 * " " * m^3 * ")")
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
```
The filtered level follows the decline around the end of the
nineteenth century while attenuating annual fluctuations.
Because each estimate uses only observations available up to
that year, adjustment to the decline occurs progressively.

The credible band becomes approximately constant in width
as the filtering variance stabilizes. It describes uncertainty
about the latent level, rather than the range of future
observed flows; observations can therefore lie outside it
without directly contradicting its stated coverage.

# One-Step-Ahead Prediction

Before observing \(y_t\), the model gives the predictive distribution

\[
y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(f_t,Q_t),
\qquad
f_t=m_{t-1},
\qquad
Q_t=C_{t-1}+W+V.
\]

The forecast mean equals the previous filtered level.
Predictive uncertainty includes uncertainty about that level,
the next state innovation, and observation noise.

```{r one-step-predictions}
forecast_mean <- as.numeric(nile_filter$f)

forecast_variance <- head(
  filter_variance_all,
  -1
) + W_known + V_known

forecast_sd <- sqrt(forecast_variance)

forecast_data <- data.frame(
  Year = nile_data$Year,
  Flow = nile_data$Flow,
  Forecast = forecast_mean,
  Lower = forecast_mean - qnorm(0.975) * forecast_sd,
  Upper = forecast_mean + qnorm(0.975) * forecast_sd
)

stopifnot(
  length(forecast_mean) == length(y),
  length(forecast_variance) == length(y),
  all(is.finite(forecast_mean)),
  all(forecast_variance > 0),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    forecast_mean,
    c(m0, head(filter_mean, -1)),
    check.attributes = FALSE
  ))
)
```

```{r one-step-prediction-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.5, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Observed Nile flow and one-step-ahead forecast means. The shaded band gives pointwise 95 percent prediction intervals for observed flow, conditional on the specified model parameters."}
ggplot(forecast_data, aes(x = Year)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper),
    fill = "#24476B",
    alpha = 0.16
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Flow, color = "Observed flow"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Forecast, color = "One-step-ahead forecast"),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed flow" = "#999999",
      "One-step-ahead forecast" = "#24476B"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1880, 1960, 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = expression("Annual flow (" * 10^8 * " " * m^3 * ")")
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
```

The forecasts follow the broad changes in flow but adjust
with a delay, since each prediction equals the previous
filtered level. This is particularly visible around the
decline at the end of the nineteenth century.

Prediction intervals are wider than the filtering credible
intervals because they describe uncertainty about an observation
not yet seen and include observation noise. Their calibration
will be examined through standardized forecast errors.

# Signal-to-Noise Sensitivity

The ratio \(W/V\) influences how strongly the filter responds
to new observations. We vary the observation variance \(V\)
while holding \(W\) fixed, and then vary \(W\) while holding
\(V\) fixed. The initial distribution remains unchanged.

The plot focuses on 1890–1950. These configurations illustrate
sensitivity to the assumed variances; they are not selected
through forecast performance.

```{r signal-to-noise-models}
sensitivity_settings <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    "Higher V",
    "Baseline",
    "Lower V",
    "Lower W",
    "Higher W"
  ),
  V = c(150000, V_known, 1500, V_known, V_known),
  W = c(W_known, W_known, W_known, W_known / 10, W_known * 10)
)

sensitivity_settings$Ratio <-
  sensitivity_settings$W / sensitivity_settings$V

sensitivity_labels <- sprintf(
  "%s (W/V = %.3f)",
  sensitivity_settings$Model,
  sensitivity_settings$Ratio
)

sensitivity_data <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(sensitivity_settings)), function(i) {
    model <- dlmModPoly(
      order = 1,
      dV = sensitivity_settings$V[i],
      dW = sensitivity_settings$W[i],
      m0 = m0,
      C0 = C0
    )

    fitted_filter <- dlmFilter(y, model)

    data.frame(
      Year = nile_data$Year,
      Forecast = as.numeric(fitted_filter$f),
      Model = sensitivity_labels[i]
    )
  })
)

sensitivity_data$Model <- factor(
  sensitivity_data$Model,
  levels = sensitivity_labels
)

sensitivity_zoom <- subset(
  sensitivity_data,
  Year >= 1890 & Year <= 1950
)

observed_zoom <- subset(
  nile_data,
  Year >= 1890 & Year <= 1950
)
```

```{r signal-to-noise-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=3, out.width="95%", fig.cap="One-step-ahead forecasts under five variance configurations, shown for 1890–1950. Observation variance V and state innovation variance W are varied separately around the baseline, keeping the initial distribution fixed."}
ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = observed_zoom,
    aes(x = Year, y = Flow),
    color = "#AAAAAA",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = sensitivity_zoom,
    aes(
      x = Year,
      y = Forecast,
      color = Model,
      linetype = Model
    ),
    linewidth = 0.55
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "#63876B", "#24476B", "#B36B35",
      "#806491", "#508C95"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "dotted", "solid", "dashed",
      "dotdash", "longdash"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1890, 1950, 10)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = expression("Annual flow (" * 10^8 * " " * m^3 * ")")
  ) +
  guides(
  color = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE),
  linetype = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
```

Increasing \(W\) or decreasing \(V\) gives new observations
more weight in the filtering update, making subsequent
forecasts more responsive to annual fluctuations. Decreasing
\(W\) or increasing \(V\) produces smoother forecasts that
adjust more slowly to changes in the observed level.

Similar ratios can produce similar forecast paths, so some
curves may overlap. However, the ratio alone does not determine
the uncertainty of the state estimates or forecasts, and the
fixed initial variance also affects the early filtering updates.

Greater responsiveness does not itself imply better forecasts:
this comparison illustrates the effect of the assumed variances,
rather than establishing which configuration predicts best.

# Forecast Error Diagnostics

We assess the baseline model using standardized one-step-ahead
forecast errors:

\[
z_t=\frac{y_t-f_t}{\sqrt{Q_t}}.
\]

Under the specified Gaussian model with known parameters,
these errors are independent standard normal variables.
We examine their time pattern, autocorrelation, and normal
quantile plot, together with a Ljung–Box test at lag 10.

These are model diagnostics on the observed sample, rather
than an independent validation of the specified variances.

```{r forecast-error-diagnostics}
forecast_errors <- as.numeric(y) - forecast_mean
standardized_errors <- forecast_errors / forecast_sd

stopifnot(
  length(standardized_errors) == length(y),
  all(is.finite(standardized_errors))
)

ljung_box <- Box.test(
  standardized_errors,
  lag = 10,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

diagnostic_summary <- data.frame(
  Diagnostic = c(
    "Mean standardized error",
    "SD of standardized errors",
    "95 percent prediction interval coverage",
    "Ljung-Box p-value (lag 10)"
  ),
  Value = c(
    mean(standardized_errors),
    sd(standardized_errors),
    mean(abs(standardized_errors) <= qnorm(0.975)),
    ljung_box$p.value
  )
)
```

```{r forecast-error-summary, results='asis'}
knitr::kable(
  diagnostic_summary,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Baseline forecast error diagnostics. Coverage is expressed as a proportion.",
  position = "H"
)
```

```{r forecast-error-plots, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=2.5, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Standardized forecast errors over time (A), their sample autocorrelation (B), and a normal quantile plot (C). Dashed ACF bounds are approximate pointwise 95 percent reference limits."}
local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  par(
    mfrow = c(1, 3),
    mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 3, 0.8),
    mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0),
    cex = 0.8
  )

  plot(
    nile_data$Year,
    standardized_errors,
    type = "l",
    col = "#243746",
    xlab = "Year",
    ylab = "Standardized error",
    main = "(A)  Forecast errors"
  )
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey60", lty = 2)

  acf(
  standardized_errors,
  lag.max = 20,
  main = "",
  xlab = "Lag",
  col = "#243746"
  )

title(main = "(B)  ACF", line = 1)

  qqnorm(
    standardized_errors,
    main = "(C)  Normal Q-Q plot",
    xlab = "Theoretical quantiles",
    ylab = "Sample quantiles",
    pch = 16,
    cex = 0.55,
    col = "#243746"
  )
  qqline(
    standardized_errors,
    col = "#B36B35",
    lwd = 1
  )
})
```
The standardized errors have mean approximately $-0.044$
and standard deviation 1.009, close to the model reference
values of zero and one. The prediction intervals contain
95 of the 100 observations.

The Ljung–Box test at lag 10 gives a p-value of 0.175,
so it does not reject the absence of autocorrelation at
the 5 percent level. The normal quantile plot is broadly
linear, with some departures in the tails.

These checks reveal no strong overall contradiction of
the baseline model, but do not establish independence,
normality, or predictive calibration in other samples.

# Smoothing

Smoothing estimates each past state using all observations,
including those recorded after that year:

\[
\theta_t \mid y_{1:T} \sim \mathcal{N}(s_t,S_t).
\]

Unlike filtering, this is a retrospective reconstruction.
The additional observations reduce state uncertainty:
\(S_t \leq C_t\). At the final observation, smoothing and
filtering coincide because no subsequent data are available.

```{r kalman-smoothing}
nile_smoother <- dlmSmooth(nile_filter)

smooth_mean <- as.numeric(dropFirst(nile_smoother$s))

smooth_covariances <- dlmSvd2var(
  nile_smoother$U.S,
  nile_smoother$D.S
)

smooth_variance_all <- vapply(
  smooth_covariances,
  function(x) as.numeric(x[1, 1]),
  numeric(1)
)

smooth_variance <- smooth_variance_all[-1]
smooth_sd <- sqrt(smooth_variance)

smoothing_data <- filter_data
smoothing_data$SmoothMean <- smooth_mean
smoothing_data$SmoothLower <-
  smooth_mean - qnorm(0.975) * smooth_sd
smoothing_data$SmoothUpper <-
  smooth_mean + qnorm(0.975) * smooth_sd

t0 <- 28L
comparison_year <- nile_data$Year[t0]

stopifnot(
  length(smooth_mean) == length(y),
  all(is.finite(smooth_mean)),
  all(is.finite(smooth_variance)),
  all(smooth_variance > 0),
  all(smooth_variance <= filter_variance + 1e-6),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    tail(smooth_mean, 1),
    tail(filter_mean, 1)
  )),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    tail(smooth_variance, 1),
    tail(filter_variance, 1)
  ))
)
```

```{r smoothing-comparison-plot, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.5, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Filtered and smoothed latent levels. The shaded band gives pointwise 95 percent smoothing credible intervals, conditional on the specified parameters. The vertical dotted line marks 1898 (t = 28)."}
ggplot(smoothing_data, aes(x = Year)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(ymin = SmoothLower, ymax = SmoothUpper),
    fill = "#24476B",
    alpha = 0.16
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Flow, color = "Observed flow"),
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Mean, color = "Filtered level"),
    linewidth = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = SmoothMean, color = "Smoothed level"),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = comparison_year,
    linetype = "dotted",
    color = "grey40",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed flow" = "#AAAAAA",
      "Filtered level" = "#B36B35",
      "Smoothed level" = "#24476B"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1880, 1960, 20)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = expression("Annual flow (" * 10^8 * " " * m^3 * ")")
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
```
The smoothed level incorporates subsequent observations and therefore
begins to decline earlier than the filtered level around 1898.
This is a retrospective revision, rather than evidence that the model
could anticipate the decline in real time.

The following comparison focuses on 1898 ($t = 28$), showing how
subsequent observations revise the estimated latent level and its
uncertainty.

```{r state-comparison-1898, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.3, out.width="75%", fig.cap="Filtered and smoothed latent-level estimates for 1898, with pointwise 95 percent credible intervals conditional on the specified parameters."}
state_comparison <- data.frame(
  Method = factor(
    c("Filtered", "Smoothed"),
    levels = c("Filtered", "Smoothed")
  ),
  Estimate = c(filter_mean[t0], smooth_mean[t0]),
  SD = c(filter_sd[t0], smooth_sd[t0])
)

state_comparison$Lower <-
  state_comparison$Estimate - qnorm(0.975) * state_comparison$SD
state_comparison$Upper <-
  state_comparison$Estimate + qnorm(0.975) * state_comparison$SD

ggplot(state_comparison, aes(x = Method, y = Estimate, color = Method)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), width = 0.12) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Filtered" = "#B36B35", "Smoothed" = "#24476B")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = expression("Annual flow (" * 10^8 * " m"^3 * ")")
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
```
For 1898, the filtered level is
`r sprintf("%.1f", state_comparison$Estimate[1])`,
with a 95 percent credible interval of
[`r sprintf("%.1f", state_comparison$Lower[1])`,
`r sprintf("%.1f", state_comparison$Upper[1])`].
Using the full series revises the estimate to
`r sprintf("%.1f", state_comparison$Estimate[2])`,
with a narrower interval of
[`r sprintf("%.1f", state_comparison$Lower[2])`,
`r sprintf("%.1f", state_comparison$Upper[2])`].
The subsequent low-flow observations pull the retrospective estimate
downward and reduce uncertainty about the latent level.

# Variance Estimation

We now estimate the observation variance $V$ and state innovation
variance $W$ by maximum likelihood, keeping the initial distribution
fixed at $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(1000,1000)$.

Optimization is performed on the logarithms of the variances to
ensure positivity. Approximate standard errors are obtained from
the inverse numerical Hessian and transformed to the variance
scale using the delta method.

```{r variance-estimation}
build_nile_model <- function(log_variances) {
  dlmModPoly(
    order = 1,
    dV = exp(log_variances[1]),
    dW = exp(log_variances[2]),
    m0 = m0,
    C0 = C0
  )
}

variance_fit <- dlmMLE(
  y,
  parm = log(c(V_known, W_known)),
  build = build_nile_model,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE,
  control = list(maxit = 1000, reltol = 1e-10)
)

stopifnot(
  variance_fit$convergence == 0,
  all(is.finite(variance_fit$par)),
  all(is.finite(variance_fit$hessian))
)

information_matrix <- (
  variance_fit$hessian + t(variance_fit$hessian)
) / 2

stopifnot(
  all(eigen(information_matrix, symmetric = TRUE)$values > 0)
)

log_variance_cov <- solve(information_matrix)
estimated_variances <- exp(variance_fit$par)

variance_se <- estimated_variances *
  sqrt(diag(log_variance_cov))

variance_table <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Observation variance V", "State innovation variance W"),
  Reference = c(V_known, W_known),
  Estimate = estimated_variances,
  SE = variance_se
)

kable(
  variance_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  position = "H",
  digits = 2,
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c(
    "Parameter", "Specified value", "MLE", "Approx. SE"
  ),
  caption = "Variance estimates conditional on the specified initial distribution."
)
```

The estimated variances are close to the specified values used
in the filtering and smoothing analysis. These estimates are
conditional on the fixed initial distribution
$\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(1000,1000)$; a different initialization
can produce different maximum-likelihood estimates.

The approximate standard error of $W$ is large relative to its
estimate, indicating substantial uncertainty about the state
innovation variance. A symmetric normal confidence interval
would extend below zero, so the standard error should be
interpreted cautiously.

The state intervals reported earlier condition on the specified
variance values and do not incorporate uncertainty about these
parameters.

# Discussion and Limitations

The local level model separates observed Nile flow into a changing
latent level and observation noise. Filtering updates the level
sequentially, while smoothing uses the full series to revise past
estimates and reduce state uncertainty. The comparison for 1898
illustrates how subsequent low-flow observations alter the
retrospective reconstruction.

The signal-to-noise ratio controls responsiveness: larger values
produce faster adjustments to new observations. Forecast-error
diagnostics reveal no strong overall contradiction with the model,
but do not establish its adequacy in other samples.

The analysis assumes Gaussian, mutually independent observation
and state innovations with constant variances. It does not explicitly
model abrupt structural changes or their causes. Variance estimates
and their approximate standard errors depend on this specification
and the fixed initial distribution. The reported state intervals
condition on the specified variances and exclude parameter uncertainty.
